eat/2026/109.rationale: This EAT decision is directly on point for the question posed. It is a leading appellate authority on the interaction between (mis)labelled self-employment, worker status and discrimination jurisdiction, and on correcting an ET's mischaracterisation of the parties' case on status.

ewca/civ/2017/51.rationale: This is the leading Court of Appeal authority on whether a plumber engaged by Pimlico Plumbers under a "self-employed contractor" agreement was a "worker" for the purposes of s.230(3) ERA 1996, reg.2(1) WTR 1998 and s.83(2)(a) Equality Act 2010 (employment for discrimination purposes). uksc/2011/40.rationale: Jivraj v Hashwani is the leading UKSC authority on precisely this question: whether a business/client who engages a tradesperson (there a solicitor, but the Court expressly considered plumbers, accountants and doctors) on a one-off contract is a "person at any time seeking to employ another" for the purposes of s.23 ERA 1996 and reg 2 of the Employment Equality (Religion or Belief) Regulations 2003, and whether the absence of an employment contract defeats the claim. The Supreme Court held that Reg 2 was not confined to a contract of employment and that the personal-service limb does not require the parties to be employer and employee, so the "plumber" scenario is squarely within the ratio. It is directly on point and binding. The provided paragraphs (7, 9-11, 24-26) set out the interpretation provisions, the EU/Regulatory background, and the Lawrie-Blum/Kurz/Allonby worker jurisprudence, but they are preparatory rather than dispositive. All three highlights from para 46 bear directly on the question: the one-off plumber contract raising the scope issue, the express statement that the Regulations may nonetheless apply to a plumber or doctor, and the key doctrinal holding that focusing solely on whether there is a contract to do work personally is the flaw in the Court of Appeal's approach.

uksc/2014/32.rationale: The question concerns a tradesperson (plumber) said to be self-employed seeking 'worker' status to bring a discrimination claim, i.e. whether actual working arrangements can confer limb (b) status despite the contract label. Clyde & Co is the leading modern UKSC restatement of the Lawrie-Blum/Allonby test (performance of services under the direction of another for remuneration, distinguished from independent providers of services not in a relationship of subordination) and is routinely cited in exactly such cases. It also confirms that the same 'worker' definition governs Equality Act 2010 discrimination claims. However, it is not directly on point: the appellant was a member of an LLP (a professional partner), not a subcontractor plumber, and the case turns on limb (b) status of LLP members and section 230(3)(a) rather than on the effect of a 'self-employed contractor' label or on the practical indicators (tools, substitution, ability to send others, invoicing) that decide plumber cases. It is therefore substantively useful background/framework authority rather than the leading case for the question.

ewca/civ/2018/2748.rationale: The question is about whether an individual whom the business has labelled a self-employed contractor nonetheless has worker status so as to bring employment/discrimination claims. It is not the specific plumber fact pattern, but the legal question (status, not trade) is directly the subject of the appeal. The highlights are all genuinely supportive: para 54 sub (a) (Autoclenz — terms of the contract may be disregarded where they artificially characterise the relationship) goes to the weight of a "self-employed contractor" label; para 39 quote (marketing oneself to the world at large as an independent business) is a key factual indicium in the multi-factor assessment; and para 128 (the Equality Act 2010 s.83(2)(a) definition is substantially the same as the s.230(3)(b) test) is directly apposite to whether a worker can bring a discrimination claim.

Mohamud v WM Morrison Supermarkets [2016] UKSC 11 was decided on 2 March 2016, satisfying the "before 2017" cut-off, and is the leading modern UK authority on vicarious liability where an employee assaults a customer.
